newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian violence, instability scare tourists.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian violence, instability scare tourists.

text.p: Foreign tourists are increasingly scarce after dark on the tense streets of Cambodia's capital Phnom Penh following the murder of an American tourist and worsening political instability, officials and tourists said on Friday.
Douglas Wayne Hosier, 36, from the state of Illinois -- his home town was not available -- was shot dead late on Wednesday during an attempted street robbery.
Late-night robberies on Phnom Penh's poorly-lit streets are not uncommon but this was the first time in recent years that a mugging ended in death.
"People are definitely scared. It really shook people up," said Bard Katveit, a 21-year-old tourist from Norway.
"I came here knowing it was a dangerous place but it seemed relaxed, but still I never go out at night alone," he told Reuters. "I also just bought a security belt for my money."
Gloomy Cambodian tourism officials said Hosier's murder was the latest blow to an already-beleaguered industry.

"One person being hurt in the streets of Phnom Penh is more than tourism can handle right now," said Sambo Chey Fennell, a senior official at the Ministry of Tourism. "Tourists fear the compounding problems here. They're afraid to go anywhere".
Ticket sales at the ancient temple of Angkor Wat, Cambodia's main tourist attraction, were down 37 percent in May and 30 percent in June compared with the same months last year, he said.
Even before this week's murder Cambodia had a reputation as one of Asia's most dangerous countries.

Three young tourists were killed after being kidnapped by Khmer Rouge guerrillas while on a train journey in southern Cambodia in 1994. Shortly before that incident three young foreigners running a restaurant in a southern beach resort were kidnapped and murdered.

Those incidents made headlines around the world but the tourism industry had actually been recovering from them, with package tourists flying in to see Angkor Wat and a steady trickle of backpackers once again passing through the country, the Tourism Ministry said.

Then, worsening political rivalry between co-premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen resulted in a June 17 gun battle in central Phnom Penh between their supporters, convincing many visitors of the risks of the city.
"I don't like being in such a lawless country," said a British backpacker in his 20s.
"I thought Cambodia was a great place. But now I see how screwed up it is. It's crazy, really mad."
Phnom Penh after dark can be an threatening place, with heavily armed security units lurking on street corners or near the homes of government officials.
But the presence of the security men has not frightened off street criminals.
A key problem for tourists and residents trying to travel around the city after dark is the absence of taxis and buses. People without cars walk or ride on the backs of motorbike taxis.
Typically, robbers will spot a foreigner on the back of a motorbike, pull up alongside with handgun drawn, force the victim's bike to stop and demand his or her valuables.
Travel agents said they were doing all they could to warn visitors to exercise caution.
"For all of our clients, we tell them to stay in their hotels in the evening. We recommend they don't go out," said Jacques Guichandut, managing director of Diethelm Travel.
